m2-electrochemical-cells: Sign of ΔG in a galvanic cell vs an electrolytic cell?
Galvanic: ΔG < 0, spontaneous, makes electricity. Electrolytic: ΔG > 0, needs an external source.
The three parts of an electrochemical cell?
Two electrodes (anode and cathode), an electrolyte (ionic conductor), and an outer electron path such as a copper wire.
In cell notation, which electrode is written on the left and what happens there?
The anode. Oxidation happens there. The cathode (reduction) goes on the right.
Daniell cell: anode, cathode and EMF?
Zn in ZnSO4 is the anode (−), Cu in CuSO4 is the cathode (+). EMF = 1.1 V.
What is the salt bridge made of, and what are its two jobs?
KCl or NH4Cl in gelatine. It keeps the charge balance in both half cells and minimises the liquid junction potential.
Define EMF of a cell.
The maximum potential difference between the two electrodes of a galvanic (voltaic) cell.
When is a cell reaction feasible?
When Ecell is positive (which means ΔG < 0).
Nernst equation when both solutions are equimolar?
Ecell = E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. The log term vanishes because log 1 = 0, so the cell potential equals the standard cell potential.
EMF of Cd | Cd<sup>2+</sup> (0.01 M) ‖ Cu<sup>2+</sup> (0.5 M) | Cu?
Who gave their names to the voltaic cell and the Daniell cell?
Alessandro Volta, Italian physicist; John Frederic Daniell, British chemist.
m2-semiconductors: Band gaps of Si and Ge as given in the slides?
Si 1.0 eV, Ge 0.7 eV. (Standard values: 1.12 eV and about 0.66 eV.)
Describe the bands of a semiconductor.
Almost filled valence band, empty conduction band, and a very narrow gap of the order of 1 eV.
Why is every semiconductor an insulator at 0 K?
Electrons are frozen in the valence band; there is no thermal energy to lift any across the gap.
What happens to a semiconductor's resistivity as temperature rises?
It decreases, so conductivity increases. Metals do the opposite.
Carrier relation in an intrinsic semiconductor?
ne = nh = ni: electrons and holes are made in pairs.
n-type: dopant type, examples, majority carrier?
Pentavalent donor (P, As, Sb); majority carriers are electrons; ne ≫ nh.
p-type: dopant type, examples, majority carrier?
Trivalent acceptor (B, Al, Ga, In); majority carriers are holes; nh ≫ ne.
What is an extrinsic semiconductor?
An intrinsic semiconductor with a small amount of impurity added (doping), which alters its electrical properties and improves conductivity.
Compound semiconductors listed in the slides?
InSb, InAs, GaP, GaSb, GaAs, SiC, GaN. Most common elemental ones: Si and Ge.
Is n-type silicon negatively charged?
No. It is electrically neutral; "n" names the majority carrier. Each free electron is balanced by a fixed P+ ion.
m2-semiconductor-purification: Purity needed for semiconductor Si and Ge?
Which compounds are distilled to purify Ge and Si?
GeCl4 for Ge (b.p. 83.1 °C per slide) and SiHCl3 (trichlorosilane) for Si.
What property does distillation exploit?
The difference in boiling points of the materials.
How is arsenic removed from GeCl<sub>4</sub>, and how is pure GeCl<sub>4</sub> then obtained?
As is removed with the help of HCl; pure GeCl4 comes from fractional distillation in the presence of chlorine.
Two reactions that turn pure GeCl<sub>4</sub> into Ge?
GeCl4 + 2H2O → GeO2 + 4HCl, then GeO2 + 2H2 → Ge + 2H2O.
Principle of zone refining?
Impurities are more soluble in the melt than in the solid. On cooling only the metal crystallises, so the moving molten zone carries impurities to the end of the ingot.
Zone refining is used to purify which elements?
Germanium, silicon, gallium, etc.
Why is Czochralski pulling needed after zone refining?
Zone-refined Ge/Si is polycrystalline. Czochralski grows a single crystal on a seed, copying its atomic arrangement.
Five stages of Czochralski growth (slide figure)?
Melting, introducing the seed, beginning of growth, crystal pulling, boule cooling.
Size of the Si crystal shown on the slide?
300 mm diameter, weight over 250 kg.
m2-batteries: The slides call the anode the "____ electrode". What actually happens to it?
Reducing electrode: it gives electrons to the external circuit, so the anode itself is oxidised.
The electrolyte's job in two words?
Ionic conductor. It carries ions but not electrons, so electrons must use the outer circuit.
Why is a primary cell "dead" at the end?
Its reaction is not reversible: once every reactant is product, no more electricity.
Three primary cells from the slides?
Leclanché (dry) cell, alkaline cell, lithium batteries.
Four secondary batteries?
Lead–acid, Ni–Cd, Ni–metal hydride, lithium-ion.
What makes flow batteries and fuel cells a separate family?
Reactants, products and electrolytes pass through the cell. Examples: HOFC, SOFC.
What kind of cell is a secondary battery while charging?
Electrolytic (it consumes electricity). While discharging it is galvanic.
Why does a fuel cell not "store" energy?
It delivers only while reactants are replenished continuously; stop the feed and the output stops.
Typical uses of primary cells?
Pacemakers, watches, transistors, radios.
The two fuel cells named in the comparison table?
H2–O2 fuel cell and CH3OH–O2 fuel cell.
m2-li-ion: Is Li-ion primary or secondary, and is there lithium metal inside?
Secondary, and it has no metallic lithium anode: lithium moves as Li+.
Who first proposed the Li-ion idea, when, and with which electrodes?
M. Whittingham, 1970s: titanium sulphide cathode, lithium metal anode.
The 2019 Chemistry Nobel for Li-ion went to?
John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, Akira Yoshino.
Li-ion maximum cell voltage vs Ni–Cd / NiMH?
3.7 V vs 1.3 V, nearly three times higher.
Specific energy density vs volumetric energy density?
Energy per unit mass vs energy per unit volume.
Why does lithium give a high cell voltage?
Li+ has a very large negative standard reduction potential.
Anode material and its usual composition?
Graphite, usually Li0.5C6.
Electrolyte and separator materials?
Electrolyte: organic carbonates (ethylene carbonate, diethyl carbonate). Separator: PE, PP or PE/PP.
During charging, which electrode is oxidised, and what do the slides call it?
LiCoO2 (cobalt ions oxidised), so it is called the anode during charging.
Which variant is "high capacity", and which is listed for electric vehicles?
LCO (LiCoO2) is high capacity (phones, laptops, cameras); NCA (LiNiCoAlO2) is for EVs and grid storage.
Li-ion cycle life and cost penalty?
500–1000 cycles; about 40% costlier than Ni–Cd.
Three causes of Li-ion explosions?
Bad design/defects (short circuit), overcharging (O2 from LiCoO2 + flammable electrolyte), electrolyte breakdown (dimethyl carbonate → CO2 pressure).
m2-fuel-cells: A fuel cell in one line?
Converts chemical potential energy (bond energy) into electrical energy without combustion.
Electrical efficiency of fuel cells vs conventional power plants?
≥ 40%, higher than conventional generation.
Which gas goes to which electrode?
Hydrogen → anode, oxygen (air) → cathode.
Why must the electrons take the external circuit?
They cannot pass through the electrolyte; only the protons can.
The eight main fuel cell types?
PEMFC, AFC, PAFC, MCFC, SOFC, DMFC, DAFC, DCFC, classified mainly by electrolyte.
Which three types are not fed with hydrogen?
DAFC (ammonia), DMFC (methanol), DCFC (carbon).
HOFC electrodes and catalyst?
Porous graphite electrodes with Pt, Ag or a metal oxide catalyst.
HOFC electrolytes?
Aqueous NaOH or KOH (alkaline, AFC) or H2SO4 (acidic).
Gas pressure in the HOFC?
About 50 atm.
Energy conversion figure on the fuel cell advantages slide?
Why are fuel cells prized in spacecraft?
Light weight, and the product water is fresh water for astronauts.
Main disadvantages of fuel cells?
High cost, durability, H2 storage, unknown lifetime, can't store electricity, expensive short-lived electrodes, flammable H2.
m2-pemfc: Proton exchange membrane fuel cell, or polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cell.
Example of the membrane, and what kind of material it is?
Nafion: a water-based, acidic polymer that conducts protons.
Why must a PEMFC run on pure hydrogen?
Its low temperature and precious-metal (Pt) electrodes leave it no tolerance for impurities.
Which ion crosses the PEMFC membrane, and where does water form?
H+ crosses anode → cathode; water forms at the cathode.
Which group in Nafion hands over the protons?
The –SO3H (sulfonic acid) groups on its side chains.
m2-sofc: YSZ, yttria-stabilized zirconia: ZrO2 stabilized with Y2O3, a solid ceramic oxide.
800–1000 °C, the highest of all fuel cell types.
Why can an SOFC run on coal gas?
It is relatively resistant to small quantities of sulphur.
Ni–YSZ cermet (nickel + YSZ; ceramic + metal), a porous layer.
A mixed ionic–electronic conducting ceramic, e.g. strontium-doped lanthanum manganite (LSM).
Bilayer YSZ + gadolinium-doped CeO2 (GDC); or a ZrO2–CaO mixture.
Which ion moves in an SOFC, and which way?
High temperature (long start-up, compatibility issues) and cost / complex fabrication.
m2-solar-energy: Theoretical solar energy potential, and where the number comes from?
1.2 × 105 TW. 1.76 × 105 TW strikes Earth and the global mean albedo of 0.30 reflects about 30% of it.
≈ 600 TW, range 50–1500 TW depending on land fraction etc. (WEA 2000).
Energy in one hour of sunlight equals...?
Onshore solar electricity potential, and the efficiency assumed?
Which solar route uses IR radiation?
Water heaters: flat plate and tube types.
The two LJSC types and their efficiencies?
Two reactions run by photoassisted electrosynthesis cells?
Three types of solar energy conversion cell?
m2-photovoltaics: Photovoltaic effect?
Creation of a voltage (or matching current) in a material on exposure to electromagnetic radiation.
Photovoltaic vs photoelectric effect?
Related but different: in the photoelectric effect the electron leaves the material; in the photovoltaic effect it stays inside and a voltage builds up.
How abundant is Si?
Second most abundant element after oxygen, ~28% by mass.
Reaction for Si from sand or quartz (as on slide 47)?
SiO2 + C → Si + CO2, heating at high temperature in a furnace.
Si band gap quoted on slide 47?
1.23 eV at 300 K. Standard value 1.12 eV, which slide 53 uses.
Dopants for Si listed on the slide?
P, As, Sb (n-type) and B, In, Al (p-type).
Single-crystal Si: efficiency and cost?
15–18%; typically expensive, grown as a big crystal.
Polycrystalline Si: efficiency and cost?
12–16%, slowly improving; cheaper, cast in ingots.
Amorphous Si: efficiency and cost?
4–8%; cheapest per watt; called "thin film", deposits on many surface types.
What is left in the depletion layer?
Fixed positive donor ions (N side) and negative acceptor ions (P side); no free carriers.
Applications of PV named on slide 52?
Aerospace and satellites.
Six disadvantages of PV?
Toxic Cd and As; light → heat; cost; variable; efficiency only 14–25%; fragile.
m2-pec-cells: Photoelectrochemical cell?
A photoactive semiconductor electrode in contact with an electrolyte; light generates a photocurrent.
Condition for making electron–hole pairs in a PEC cell?
Light energy greater than Eg of the semiconductor.
What separates the pairs, and what do they then do?
The junction potential; the separated charges drive oxidation and reduction.
LJSC construction and output?
n-SC / Electrolyte / Metal; solar → electrical energy.
What does a PES cell do?
Converts solar energy into chemical energy in the form of fuels.
Four requirements for PEC electrodes?
Optimum Eg; optimum doping; large α; applied bias.
Why should the doping level be optimum?
Good spatial separation of photo-generated carriers, hence high quantum efficiency.
Large absorption coefficient α is usually found in?
Direct band gap semiconductors.
What makes a PEC cell "regenerative"?
Red → Ox at the SC and Ox → Red at the counter electrode: no net chemical change, only electricity out.
Five advantages of PEC over PV?
Easy junction (dipping); in-situ water electrolysis; poly/thin film ≈ single crystal; photocatalysis and novel products; particulate systems.
m2-dssc: Four basic steps of DSSC operation?
Light absorption, electron injection, carrier transport, current collection (then dye regeneration).
Dye excitation and injection equations (slide 70)?
Dyeo + hν → Dye*; Dye* → Dye*+ + e− (TiO2).
Lifetime of the excited electrons, and where they go?
Nanosecond range; injected into the conduction band of nanoporous TiO2, which lies below Dye*.
How is the oxidised dye regenerated?
I− gives it electrons and is oxidised (loses 2 e−) to I3−; I3− is reduced back at the graphite (or Pt) plate.
ITO vs FTO numbers?
ITO: > 80% transmittance, 18 Ω/cm2. FTO: ~75%, 8.5 Ω/cm2. Both on soda lime glass.
Working-electrode oxides and their band gap?
TiO2, Nb2O5, ZnO, SnO2 (n-type), NiO (p-type); 3–3.2 eV.
Why is TiO₂ the usual choice?
Non-toxic and easily available; porous, high-area film holds lots of dye.
Properties of a good DSSC dye?
Luminescent; absorbs UV-vis and NIR; hydrophobic periphery; CDCA or anchoring groups (alkoxy-silyl, phosphoric acid, –COOH) to prevent aggregation.
Five main components of a DSSC electrolyte?
Redox couple, solvent, additives, ionic liquids, cations.
Counter-electrode materials?
Pt, C, CoS, Au/GNP; alloys FeSe and CoNi0.25.
Dye solution used for the hibiscus-tea cell?
10−4 M in alcohol, about 10 min; upper TiO2 plate = anode, lower graphite plate = cathode.
Main disadvantages of a DSSC?
Liquid electrolyte with temperature stability problems, costly Ru dye and Pt catalyst, VOCs in the electrolyte.
m3-nanomaterials: What size rule makes something a nanomaterial?
At least one dimension below about 100 nm.
1 nm in metres and in millimetres?
10−9 m, which is one millionth of a millimetre.
About how many atoms side by side make 1 nm?
10. One atom is about 0.1 nm.
Diameter of a human hair in nanometres?
50,000–100,000 nm. A nanometre is about 100,000 times smaller.
What is an engineered nanomaterial (EN)?
A nanomaterial designed on purpose for commercial products and processes, as opposed to one that occurs naturally.
Uses of nanoscale TiO<sub>2</sub>?
Cosmetics, sun-block creams and self-cleaning windows.
What is nanoscale silica used for?
As a filler in cosmetics and dental fillings.
What makes some tennis balls last longer?
A butyl-rubber / nano-clay composite.
Three medical uses of nanomaterials?
Diagnosis, imaging and drug delivery.
Name the five nanodevices on the slide-5 scale chart.
Nanopores, dendrimers, nanotubes, quantum dots, nanoshells.
m3-nano-classes: What does the "D" number in 0D–3D count?
The number of free dimensions: dimensions allowed outside the nanoscale.
All three dimensions in the nanoscale. Nanoparticles, colloids, quantum dots.
One dimension beyond the nanoscale, two inside. Nanowires, nanorods, nanotubes, biopolymers.
One dimension in the nanoscale, any two outside. Plate-like: nanolayers, surface coatings, thin films.
All three dimensions outside the nanoscale, but made of nanomaterials. Nanoparticle dispersions, nanowire/nanotube bundles, multiple nanolayers.
Metal oxides (ZnO, iron oxide, cerium oxide), metals (Au, Ag, Fe), quantum dots (CdS, CdSe).
Fullerenes and carbon nanotubes belong to which category?
m3-nano-gold: Why are nanophase ceramics interesting?
They are more ductile at high temperatures than coarse-grained ceramics.
What is nanostructured MnO<sub>2</sub> used for?
Rechargeable batteries for cars and consumer goods.
What gives very small particles their special properties, per slide 10?
Special atomic structures with discrete electronic states, plus superparamagnetism.
Colour reflected by gold spheres in glass at 25, 50 and 100 nm?
Red, green, orange.
Colour of silver particles in glass: 40 nm sphere, 100 nm sphere, 100 nm prism?
Blue, yellow, red.
What is surface plasmon resonance?
Light's electromagnetic field drives a collective oscillation of surface electrons; certain wavelengths are absorbed and the rest scattered or reflected, giving the colour.
What does the colour of metal nanoparticles depend on?
Size, shape and material, and the distance between particles.
Melting point of bulk vs nano gold (slide values)?
How does the slide describe nano gold electrically?
Not a metal but a semiconductor, band gap 3.4 eV (slide value).
Bulk gold is inert. What is nano gold instead?
A very good catalyst.
m3-why-nano: Two main reasons nanomaterials have different properties?
Increased relative surface area and new quantum effects.
Total area of a 1 cm cube, then cut into 8, then 27 equal cubes?
6 cm², 12 cm², 18 cm². Volume stays 1 cm³.
What stays constant when a bulk solid is subdivided into nanoparticles?
The total volume. Only the collective surface area grows.
Main practical gain from a higher surface area / volume ratio?
Better catalytic efficiency.
What happens to light behaviour when electron movement is restricted?
Particles react differently with light, giving tunable fluorescent emission.
Define quantum confinement.
The spatial confinement of electrons in a nanomaterial rather than their free existence within the bulk.
When do electron–hole pairs become confined?
When the particle diameter approaches the de Broglie wavelength of conduction-band electrons.
What does quantum confinement do to the energy gap, and what transition follows?
Increases the gap, giving a metal → semiconductor → insulator transition.
Why are nanomaterials mechanically stronger?
Fewer imperfections and defects, so more structural perfection (higher hardness, toughness).
Biological property change at the nanoscale?
Permeability through biological membranes increases because of the smaller size.
m3-synthesis: Top-down approach: what is it and what is it good for?
Breaking larger pieces down into nanostructures. Good for long-range order and macroscopic connections.
Bottom-up approach: what is it and what is it good for?
Assembling single atoms and molecules into nanostructures. Best for assembly and short-range order.
What kinds of methods does bottom-up use?
Mechanical milling, etching, laser ablation, sputtering, electro-explosion.
Supercritical fluid synthesis, spinning, sol–gel, laser pyrolysis, CVD, molecular condensation, chemical reduction, green synthesis.
Intermediate stage in top-down vs bottom-up?
m3-milling: Two other names for mechanical milling?
Top-down or bottom-up? How does it reduce size?
Starting powder size and ball materials?
About 50 µm; hardened steel or tungsten carbide (WC) coated balls.
Most effective ball-to-powder mass ratio, as printed on the slide?
Batch size in a SPEX 8000 shaker mill?
Temperature generated at the interphase during milling?
Fe < 1–2%, trace elements < 300 ppm; inert conditions (glove box) needed.
What happens to milling-tool contamination after more than 30 h?
Three product families made by milling?
Oxide/carbide-strengthened Al alloys, Al/Ni/Mg/Cu nanoalloys and nanocomposites, ball-milled carbon for remediation, energy storage and conversion.
m3-sol-gel: Is sol–gel top-down or bottom-up, and what does it mainly make?
Bottom-up; high-quality metal-oxide nanomaterials.
Conventional precursors for sol–gel?
Metal alkoxides, M(OR)n.
What are a sol and a gel?
Sol: solid particles in solution. Gel: the network structure the sol turns into.
The five sol–gel steps in order?
Hydrolysis → condensation → aging → drying → calcination.
Generic hydrolysis reaction?
–M–OR + H2O → –M–OH + ROH
Two condensation routes and their by-products?
–M–OH + RO–M– → –M–O–M– + ROH; –M–OH + HO–M– → –M–O–M– + H2O.
Which bridges form during condensation?
Hydroxo (M–OH–M) or oxo (M–O–M) bridges, giving metal–hydroxo or metal–oxo polymers.
What changes during aging?
Polycondensation continues; porosity decreases and the distance between colloidal particles increases.
What does drying remove, and what does calcination give?
Drying removes water and organic solvents; calcination gives the nanoparticles.
Film route vs bulk route after the sol?
Films: spin- or dip-coating → xerogel film → dense film. Bulk: gel → xerogel → dense ceramic.
Two advantages of sol–gel?
Glasses and ceramics at very low temperatures; monosized nanoparticles.
Four disadvantages of sol–gel?
Controlling growth and agglomeration; incomplete reaction leaves reactant; removing growth aids; very slow production.
m3-quantum-dots: Size range of a quantum dot?
2–10 nm in diameter, about 10–50 atoms across.
How many electrons does a quantum dot contain?
100 to 1000 electrons.
Three example QD materials?
CdSe (cadmium selenide), CdS (cadmium sulfide), InP (indium phosphide).
What decides the colour a QD emits?
The amount of energy released when electrons drop back, which is set by the size of the dot.
2–3 nm dot vs 5–6 nm dot: which colours?
2–3 nm: blue / violet (higher energy). 5–6 nm: red / orange (lower energy).
What happens to the band gap and emission as a QD grows?
Band gap decreases; emission is red-shifted (longer wavelength).
Define quantum confinement.
Spatial confinement of electrons in a nanomaterial, instead of their free existence in the bulk.
When does quantum confinement set in?
When the particle diameter approaches the de Broglie wavelength of the conduction-band electrons.
Schrödinger's point about confined electrons?
Electrons in confined systems occupy quantised energy levels.
Bulk semiconductor vs QD energy levels?
Bulk: continuous levels in bands. QD: discrete levels and a large band gap.
Four properties of QDs?
High extinction coefficient, high electron mobility, bandwidth and position adjustment, solution process capabilities.
Why does one batch of QDs glow a single colour?
The quantised gap makes the energy released nearly the same from electron to electron, so emission is at a very constant wavelength.
m3-qd-uses: Four synthesis routes for QDs?
High temperature, hydrothermal, microwave and ultrasonication synthesis.
Conditions in high temperature QD synthesis?
Heating mantle above 200 °C, high-boiling-point solvent, precursors injected by syringe, N2 atmosphere, temperature sensor.
Vessel used in hydrothermal synthesis?
A Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave with a Teflon cap and stainless steel plates.
Layers of a core–shell quantum dot?
Core, shell, then an outer coat: ligands (synthesis figure) or a protective shell.
How do QDs help solar cells?
They absorb a wider range of light wavelengths, raising efficiency.
Which TVs use QDs?
QD-OLED TVs: brighter, more vibrant colours.
Biomedical use of QDs?
Imaging tissues and cells, aiding diagnostics and drug delivery.
Uses of QDs still being explored?
Sensors, lasers, quantum computing and other research areas.
How can QDs detect metal ions such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> or Pb<sup>2+</sup>?
The ion binds to the dot surface and changes its emission (dims or shifts the colour): metal ions sensing.
m3-coolants: What is a coolant?
A fluid that runs across an engine, absorbs heat, carries it to the radiator to be cooled, and is recycled.
Where are coolants used?
Automobiles, HVAC, home ACs, computers, supercomputers, data centres, miniature electronics, military and mobile devices.
Heat flux a power-dense chip can produce?
Up to 1000 W/cm2.
Five thermophysical properties that matter in a coolant?
Thermal conductivity, specific heat, latent heat of vaporization, surface tension, viscosity.
Why are non-aqueous coolants preferred around electronics?
Water and glycol–water are highly conductive; a spill may damage the electronics.
Flash point rule for flammability?
Flash point below 93 °C = flammable.
Three common flammable liquids that fail the flash-point test?
Ethanol, methanol, benzene.
Which coolants have low toxicity compared with ethylene glycol?
Fluorocarbon and hydrofluoroether coolants.
Preferred device materials and why?
Copper and aluminium: high thermal conductivity, compatible with most coolants.
PFC vs HFE: GWP and ODP?
PFC: high GWP, zero ODP. HFE: low GWP, zero ODP.
What raises the cost of water-based coolants?
Adding antifreeze, glycols and anti-corrosion materials.
m3-coolant-types: Four thermal strengths of water as a coolant?
Good thermal conductivity, high specific heat, high latent heat of vaporization, low viscosity.
Water's main drawback and the usual fix?
It freezes; additives such as glycol lower the freezing point.
Problem with water–NaCl or water–CaCl<sub>2</sub>?
Low freezing point, but salt solutions are highly corrosive.
Why add corrosion inhibitors even to deionised water?
Exposure to air can make it corrosive.
Three common corrosion inhibitors?
Phosphates, tolyltriazole, 2-ethylhexanoic acid.
Two water–glycol coolants?
Water–ethylene glycol and water–propylene glycol: lower freezing point than water.
Water–potassium formate/acetate: freezing point and users?
−70 °C; used in food, beverage, chemical and pharmaceutical industries. Less corrosive than NaCl/CaCl2 brines.
Where do data centres use dielectric coolants?
Immersion cooling or direct-to-chip cooling.
Four families of dielectric coolants?
Aromatics, aliphatic, fluorocarbons (HFE, PFC), silicones.
Examples of HFE and PFC coolants?
m4-spectroscopy: Spectroscopy is the interaction of ___ with ___.
Electromagnetic radiant energy with matter.
Who introduced the word "spectrum", and when?
Sir Isaac Newton, 1672, to describe the rainbow of colours.
Fraunhofer and Kirchhoff: years and contributions?
Fraunhofer 1814: optics and spectroscopy. Kirchhoff 1859: showed spectroscopy is useful for chemical analysis.
Three ways energy is transferred?
Conduction (direct contact), convection (through a fluid by molecular motion), radiation (rays, waves or particles).
Dual nature of radiation: who, when, and what does it say?
de Broglie, 1923. EMR behaves as a wave in space and as a particle (photons) in matter interaction.
Which nature of light explains reflection, refraction and diffraction? Which explains absorption and emission?
Wave nature for the first three; particle (photon) nature for absorption and emission.
Speed of light in vacuum on the slides?
c = 2.9979 × 108 m s−1 (rounded to 3.00 × 108 in the numericals).
Energy of a photon in terms of frequency?
E = hν: directly proportional to frequency. Photons are discrete packets of energy.
Transmission vs scattering?
Transmission: radiation passes through without measurable attenuation. Scattering: energy is re-radiated in different directions, off the original path.
What does a spectrum plot?
The sample's response as a function of wavelength or frequency.
m4-emr-regions: UV-visible radiation: energy range and what it changes?
103–101 kJ/mol; causes electronic transitions (UV-Vis spectroscopy).
Infrared: energy and effect?
101–10−1 kJ/mol; vibrational transitions (IR spectroscopy).
Microwaves and radiowaves: which techniques, per the slide table?
Microwaves (10−3 kJ/mol): ESR, rotational motion. Radiowaves (10−7 kJ/mol): NMR, nuclear spin transitions.
1 eV in kJ/mol?
The radio row of the regions table: λ, ν, E and application?
λ > 109 Å, ν < 3 × 109 Hz, E < 10−5 eV; nuclear effect; used for molecular identity and structure.
State the principle of spectroscopy as an equation.
hν = ΔE = E1 − E0: the photon energy must equal the gap between the two states.
Atomic vs molecular spectra: which gives lines and which gives bands, and why?
Atomic: line spectrum (electronic transitions only). Molecular: band spectrum (electronic + vibrational + rotational sub-levels).
Examples of atomic and molecular absorption and emission spectroscopy?
Atomic: atomic absorption, flame emission. Molecular: UV-Vis, IR (absorption), fluorescence, phosphorescence (emission).
ν of radiation with λ = 5.00 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m? Region?
6.00 × 1015 s−1, ultraviolet (slide: middle UV).
λ of radiation from radioactive cobalt, ν = 2.80 × 10<sup>20</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>? Region?
1.07 × 10−12 m, gamma rays.
Mini-TES, MB and APXS on the Mars rovers: what does each examine?
Mini-TES: rock, soil and atmosphere. MB (Mössbauer): mineralogy. APXS (Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer): elements in rocks and soils.
Non-EM probes in the spectroscopy family tree?
Alpha particles, beta particles, protons, neutrons (radiography, neutron spectroscopy, neutron-induced gamma spectroscopy), acoustic and seismic waves.
m4-uv-vis: UV-Vis spectroscopy covers which wavelength range, and what does the light do?
200–700 nm; it excites valence electrons (electronic excitation).
UVA, UVB, UVC: other names and ozone behaviour?
UVA (near, long-wave, black light): not absorbed by O3. UVB (medium-wave): mostly absorbed. UVC (far, short-wave, ionizing): absorbed.
Condition for absorption between S<sub>0</sub> and S<sub>1</sub>?
hν = ΔS = S1 − S0
Fluorescence vs phosphorescence?
Fluorescence: S1 → S0, fast. Phosphorescence: T1 → S0 after intersystem crossing, slow.
σ → σ*: where and what range?
Only simple bonds (C–H, C–C); high energy, 100–150 nm.
n → σ*: where and what range?
Atoms with lone pairs (N, O, S); 150–250 nm.
π → π* and n → π*: ranges?
π → π* (unsaturated/aromatics): 200–700 nm. n → π* (lone pair + unsaturation): 250–500 nm.
Energy order of the four transitions?
σ → σ* > n → σ* > π → π* > n → π*
The four ε classes?
Forbidden ε ≤ 10; partly allowed 10–1000; allowed 1000–100000; highly allowed ≥ 100000.
Chromophore vs auxochrome, with examples.
Chromophore: isolated unsaturated group that absorbs (>C=C<, >C=O, –N=N–, –NO2). Auxochrome: attached group that modifies absorption (–COOH, –OH, –SO3H, –NR2, –NH2).
Bathochromic, hypsochromic, hyperchromic, hypochromic?
Red shift (longer λ), blue shift (shorter λ), intensity up, intensity down.
Why does methylene blue look blue?
It absorbs 600–700 nm (orange-red); we see the complementary colour, blue.
m4-beer-lambert: State the Beer–Lambert law as an equation.
What does the law say, in words?
At a wavelength maximum, absorption is proportional to concentration of absorbing molecules and to path length.
Units of L, C and ε?
L in cm; C in mol/L; ε in L mol−1 cm−1.
Other name and the people/years behind it?
Does the law only work for visible light?
No: it applies to all forms of electromagnetic radiation.

m4-uv-vis-instrument: Who created spectrophotometry, and when (per the slides)?
Arnold O. Beckman, 1940.
Parts of a single-beam spectrophotometer?
Polychromatic source, wavelength selector (and eventually a source selector), sample compartment, detector, screen and/or computer.
Which two lamps does the double-beam instrument use?
D2 (deuterium) lamp for UV and tungsten lamp for visible.
What does the beam splitter do in a double-beam instrument, and why is that useful?
Sends light through the sample and the reference at the same time; comparing them cancels lamp drift and solvent absorption.
λ<sub>max</sub> used for vitamins A<sub>1</sub> and A<sub>2</sub>?
A1: 325 nm; A2: 351 nm.
An organic compound shows no λ<sub>max</sub> above 200 nm. What can you conclude?
It contains no conjugated chromophore, aldehyde, keto group or benzene ring.
Cis vs trans in UV-Vis?
Trans shows the longer wavelength and higher intensity.
Keto vs enol bands?
Keto: 275 nm, ε = 20 (isolated C=O). Enol: 245 nm, ε = 1800 (conjugated double bond).
What does a charge-transfer complex show in UV-Vis?
New absorption peaks, from an electron donor–acceptor pair.
Transitions possible in dimethyl ether?
σ → σ* and n → σ* (σ bonds + O lone pairs, no π bond).
m4-xrays: Wavelength range of X-rays, and where that sits?
0.01–10 nm: shorter than UV, longer than gamma.
Energy and frequency range of X-rays?
Who discovered X-rays, when, and when was the Nobel?
W.C. Röntgen, 1895; Nobel Prize 1901.
Hard vs soft X-ray ranges (as given)?
Hard 0.01–1 nm, soft 0.1–10 nm. Analytical work: 0.7–2 nm on the page, meant as 0.7–2 Å.
Whose hand is in the first radiograph of a human body?
Anna Bertha Ludwig, Röntgen's wife.
Cathode, anode and voltage in an X-ray tube?
Cathode (−) W filament; anode (+) Cu/Cr/Mo/W disk; 25–150 kV; evacuated bulb.
Five features that make tungsten the filament?
Z = 74, efficient electron release, good thermionic emitter, made as thin wires, M.P. 3422 °C.
How are continuous X-rays made, and who found the effect?
An electron is decelerated in the field of a nucleus; lost KE comes out as polychromatic "white" X-rays. Nikola Tesla.
Kα vs Kβ?
Kα: L → K drop. Kβ: M → K drop (bigger gap, shorter λ).
Cu Kα energy and wavelength?
Who discovered characteristic X-rays and when?
Charles Glover Barkla, 1909.
Kα (Å) of Cr, Fe, Co, Cu, Mo as listed?
m4-bragg: When does diffraction occur?
When a wave passes a slit or corner smaller than or equal to its wavelength.
Everyday example of diffraction on the page?
Light bending around the corners of doors and windows.
Constructive vs destructive interference?
Constructive: waves in phase, greater amplitude. Destructive: out of phase, cancel, no net motion.
Crystalline, polycrystalline, amorphous?
Orderly array throughout; ordered in segments; no long-range order.
Why do quartz, cristobalite and glass give different XRD patterns?
Same formula SiO2, different structures: quartz and cristobalite give sharp peaks, glass a broad hump.
The three-part rule behind XRD?
Every crystalline substance gives a pattern; the same substance always gives the same pattern; in a mixture each gives its pattern independently.
Path difference in the Bragg derivation?
δ = CB + BD = d sin θ + d sin θ = 2d sin θ.
Bragg's law and its symbols?
2d sin θ = nλ: d plane spacing, θ angle to the planes, λ wavelength, n integer (1, 2, 3…).
Nobel Prizes linked to XRD?
Max von Laue 1914 (X-ray diffraction); W.H. and W.L. Bragg 1915 (crystal structure analysis).
d for λ = 0.9 Å, θ = 7°, n = 1?
d = 0.9 / (2 × 0.1218) = 3.69 Å (page wrongly writes 10−10 cm).
m4-xrd-patterns: What does an X-ray diffractometer do?
Produces monochromatic X-rays, focuses them on the sample, scans a 2θ range, detects reflected X-rays and their intensity, shows a diffractogram.
Order of parts from tube to PC?
HV supply → X-ray tube → primary filter → collimator → sample → detector & pre-amp → main amplifier → amplitude analyzer → control unit → communication module → PC.
Three detector types?
Gas-filled, scintillation, semiconductor.
Why is the diffractometer attached to a goniometer?
For simultaneous scanning: sample turns θ while the detector turns 2θ.
What does peak position tell you?
Where atoms sit in the lattice, via the d-spacing (Bragg).
What does peak intensity tell you?
The number of atoms in phase; higher = more crystals/molecules with that spacing.
A broad peak suggests…
Smaller crystal, defects, or amorphous nature (width ∝ 1/size).
JCPDS and ICSD stand for?
Joint Committee on Powder Diffraction Standards; International (officially Inorganic) Crystal Structure Database.
NaCl reference data on the page?
FCC, a = b = c = 5.64 Å, α = β = γ = 90°, ρ = 2.14 g/cm3; strongest peak (200).
Four applications of XRD?
Crystalline vs amorphous; unit cell, atom positions, symmetry; texture of polygrained materials; strain and small grain size.
Advantages and the main disadvantage of XRD?
Lowest cost and convenient; no evacuated chamber; nondestructive. Weak with lighter elements.
m4-scherrer: What is a crystallite, and how is its size found?
A small crystal of many atoms/molecules that diffracts coherently; size from the XRD peak via Scherrer's formula.
How do grains form, and what sees them?
From multiple nucleation centres during crystal growth; each holds many crystallites; measured by SEM.
What is a particle, and what sees it?
A single crystal or an agglomeration of grains; always larger than a crystallite; measured by TEM.
Correct size order (the page prints it reversed)?
Particle ≥ grain ≥ crystallite > unit cell.
Scherrer equation and its terms?
D = kλ / β cos θ: β = FWHM in radians, θ = Bragg angle, λ = X-ray wavelength, k = shape constant.
Value of k for FWHM of spherical cubic crystals?
0.94 (k depends on shape).
What is FWHM?
Full width at half maximum: peak width at Imax/2 above background.
